content: Specimens that test positive for MERS-CoV should undergo genetic sequencing, and the resulting data should be uploaded to publicly accessible databases. If the initial testing laboratory lacks the capacity for genetic sequencing, an aliquot of the specimen should be sent to a reference laboratory. These reference centers should aim to isolate the virus from all cases to enable whole genome sequencing, which can be performed either at national or international reference laboratories. These include the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) during patient care and the isolation of confirmed and probable cases. Additionally, strict infection control and PPE use are required during the collection, transportation, and testing of laboratory specimens from patients suspected of MERS-CoV infection. However, due to the potential for rapid progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and other severe complications, even otherwise healthy symptomatic contacts or probable cases should be closely monitored in a medical facility. Data analysis plans should align with the objectives of the investigation. At a minimum, descriptive analyses of cases should be conducted, focusing on person, place, and time (e.g., age and sex distribution). Parameters such as incubation periods, transmission patterns, attack rates by age or occupation, and illness severity should be characterized to enhance understanding of the disease dynamics associated with MERS-CoV infection. Specific studies are necessary to address critical public health questions about MERS-CoV. Healthcare-associated outbreaks of MERS-CoV have been reported, with human-to-human transmission occurring among healthcare workers, patients, and visitors. Ideally, these studies should be conducted prospectively as soon as MERS-CoV infection is suspected. Investigations into recent respiratory disease trends should include a review of surveillance data for severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) and other relevant conditions. Stored specimens from SARI cases should be tested for MERS-CoV. Hospital admission records, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs), should be reviewed for unexplained respiratory infections or pneumonia. Outpatient clinic records should also be examined for increases in respiratory illnesses or influenza-like symptoms. Any unexplained cases should be tested for MERS-CoV. Seroprevalence studies can help estimate the prevalence of antibodies against MERS-CoV in specific populations, such as market workers, farm workers, and healthcare workers. These studies can identify activities associated with an increased risk of infection and provide insights into the relative risk of infection among different groups. Cross-sectional seroprevalence surveys conducted early in an outbreak can be compared to later surveys to estimate the incidence of infection over time. Clinical management of MERS-CoV infection focuses on supportive care for patients with acute respiratory failure and septic shock. While specific treatments have been studied in cell cultures, convalescent sera from recovered patients show the most promise, though further research is needed. Clinical management protocols are being developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), and investigators are encouraged to collaborate with WHO for guidance. WHO requests that probable and confirmed MERS-CoV cases be reported within 24 hours of classification through the appropriate regional contact point for International Health Regulations. Early reporting of investigation results, even if preliminary, is strongly encouraged to aid in the assessment of international spread and inform decision-making. WHO has established networks to support investigators in conducting studies and interpreting results. Coordination between human and animal investigations is critical, and guidance from organizations such as the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) should be sought for technical issues related to disease surveillance, prevention, and control in animals.
